title: Coupling in Distributed Systems
body:
# Coupling in Distributed Systems

<BurgerAnalogy text={"If our burger restaurant accepts an order only after one specific kitchen station answers immediately, the counter depends tightly on that station. A shared order format and a directory of available stations make replacements easier. This reduces coupling, but someone must still maintain the contracts and discovery process; fewer direct dependencies do not remove the need for coordination."} />

Coupling measures how tightly components in a system are connected or dependent. In distributed systems, its type and level have a strong impact on flexibility, maintainability, and resilience.

<Callout type="info" title="💡 Key Concept">

Lower coupling increases flexibility and maintainability, but extremely low coupling can add complexity. Balance is essential.

</Callout>

## Types of Coupling

### Static Coupling

Static coupling connects components at compile time, creating fixed dependencies that are difficult to change without modifying the code.

<Cards cols={2}>

<Card title="Characteristics" accent="brand">

- **Direct dependencies** — Explicit references to specific classes or modules
- **Compile-time checks** — Errors are detected before execution
- **Less flexibility** — Changes require recompilation and redeployment

</Card>

<Card title="Advantages" accent="brand">

**Advantages**

- Early error detection
- Better runtime performance
- Easier to understand and trace

**Disadvantages**

- Less flexibility when making changes
- More difficult maintenance
- Less resilience to failures

</Card>

</Cards>

**Static Coupling Example:**

```ts
// Static coupling through a direct import
import { UserService } from './UserService';

class OrderProcessor {
  private userService: UserService;

  constructor() {
    // Fixed, direct dependency
    this.userService = new UserService();
  }

  async processOrder(orderId: string) {
    // If UserService is unavailable, there is no alternative
    const user = await this.userService.getUser(orderId);
    // Process the order...
  }
}
```

### Dynamic Coupling

Dynamic coupling connects components at runtime, offering greater flexibility and allowing implementations to change without recompilation.

<Cards cols={2}>

<Card title="Characteristics" accent="purple">

- **Runtime discovery** — Services are discovered and connected dynamically
- **Greater flexibility** — Implementations can be replaced at runtime
- **Resilience** — Better adaptation to failures and changes

</Card>

<Card title="Advantages / Disadvantages" accent="purple">

**Advantages**

- Greater flexibility and adaptability
- Better resilience to failures
- Easier maintenance and evolution

**Disadvantages**

- Greater implementation complexity
- Possible runtime failures
- Performance overhead

</Card>

</Cards>

**Dynamic Coupling Example:**

```ts
// Dynamic coupling using dependency injection and service discovery
interface UserServiceInterface {
  getUser(id: string): Promise<User>;
}

class OrderProcessor {
  private userService: UserServiceInterface;
  private serviceRegistry: ServiceRegistry;

  constructor(serviceRegistry: ServiceRegistry) {
    this.serviceRegistry = serviceRegistry;
  }

  async processOrder(orderId: string) {
    try {
      // Discover the service dynamically
      this.userService = await this.serviceRegistry.getService('UserService');
      const user = await this.userService.getUser(orderId);
    } catch (error) {
      // Fall back to an alternative service
      this.userService = await this.serviceRegistry.getBackupService('UserService');
      const user = await this.userService.getUser(orderId);
    }
    // Process the order...
  }
}
```

### Service Discovery

Service Discovery is a fundamental pattern to enable dynamic coupling in distributed systems. It lets services find and communicate with each other without prior knowledge of locations.

<Cards cols={2}>

<Card title="Main Components" accent="green">

- **Service registry** — Where services register when they start
- **Health checking** — Monitoring service health
- **Dynamic DNS** — Dynamic address resolution

</Card>

<Card title="Popular Tools" accent="green">

- **Consul** — A solution for service discovery, configuration, and segmentation
- **Eureka** — Netflix service discovery for Java applications
- **etcd** — Distributed key-value storage used by Kubernetes

</Card>

</Cards>

## Best Practices

<Cards cols={2}>

<Card title="Design & Architecture" accent="brand">

- **Well-defined interfaces** — Use interfaces to define clear contracts between services
- **Dependency injection** — Use DI to manage dependencies flexibly
- **Appropriate abstraction** — Find the right level of abstraction for each component

</Card>

<Card title="Implementation" accent="purple">

- **Service discovery** — Implement robust service discovery mechanisms
- **Circuit breakers** — Use circuit breakers to handle service failures
- **Fallbacks** — Implement fallback strategies for greater resilience

</Card>

</Cards>

## Trade-offs and Considerations

<Cards cols={3}>

<Card title="Performance" accent="brand">

- Static coupling generally has lower runtime overhead
- Dynamic coupling adds discovery overhead
- Consider the impact on latency and throughput

</Card>

<Card title="Complexity" accent="purple">

- Dynamic coupling increases complexity
- Distributed state must be managed
- A steeper learning curve for the team

</Card>

<Card title="Maintainability" accent="green">

- Loose coupling makes changes easier
- Isolated testing is easier
- Better support for parallel development

</Card>

</Cards>

## Real-World Examples

### Microservices at Netflix

Netflix illustrates dynamic coupling in microservice architectures. Eureka provides service discovery, and Hystrix is a historical example of circuit breaking.

```java
@EnableEurekaClient
public class VideoServiceApplication {
    @Bean
    @LoadBalanced
    public RestTemplate restTemplate() {
        return new RestTemplate();
    }
}
```

### Kubernetes Service Discovery

Kubernetes implements service discovery through its internal DNS and Services, allowing pods to communicate without knowing specific instance locations.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: user-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: user-service
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
```
